objections.title: Only science gives real knowledge (scientism)
objections.whoRaises: Alex Rosenberg; the New Atheists generally; many scientifically educated skeptics
objections.objection: Science is the only reliable way to know anything about reality, and our best scientific theories nowhere mention God. So natural theology isn’t even in the running: whatever it offers is speculation, not knowledge, and can be set aside without examination.
objections.reply:
Feser’s central reply is a dilemma.

1. **Taken strictly, scientism refutes itself.** The claim that only science yields knowledge is not a finding of science — no experiment establishes it. Science also rests on assumptions it can’t prove without circularity: that there is a mind-independent world, that it is orderly, and that our minds and senses can grasp it. Justifying those requires a standpoint outside science, and the existence of such a standpoint falsifies scientism.
2. **Science needs philosophy at both ends.** Beyond its presuppositions, science needs philosophy to interpret its results — what causation is, whether the world is substances or events, what the universals in laws are, whether theories describe reality or just predict. So scientism is doubly false.
3. **Taken broadly, scientism is empty.** If the advocate says philosophy counts as “science,” he has redefined the word to include anything that might be offered against him — including natural theology, which Aristotle and Aquinas considered a science more certain than physics, since it demonstrates from premises every physical science presupposes. Then scientism can no longer be used to dismiss natural theology unheard.

Either way, the critic has to engage the arguments rather than rule them out by definition.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says, “Fine, but science is still the *best* guide we have,” agree that it is the best guide to what it studies — the measurable and predictable — and ask what experiment showed that it is the best guide to everything, including the question of whether it is the best guide to everything.

> One-liner: “Only science gives knowledge” isn’t something science discovered — so by its own rule, you couldn’t know it.

objections.title: Science’s unmatched success shows it tells the whole story
objections.whoRaises: Alex Rosenberg, *The Atheist’s Guide to Reality*; widely assumed in popular science writing
objections.objection: Physics predicts with astonishing accuracy and gives us technology that works. That would be a miracle unless its methods were the right ones for all knowledge. So what science reveals is probably all that is real; carving out some domain exempt from it is special pleading.
objections.reply:
Feser reduces the argument to two steps — science’s predictive and technological success is unparalleled; therefore what science reveals is probably all there is — and shows it has the same form as an obviously bad argument: metal detectors outperform every other way of finding metal, so metal is probably all that exists.

- A method’s success at capturing one aspect of reality — for physics, the aspects that can be modeled mathematically and so predicted and controlled — does nothing to show there are no other aspects.
- Physics succeeds precisely *because* it restricts itself to the quantifiable. Like the airplane engineers who treat passengers as average weights, it leaves out qualities, purposes, and meanings by design, so their absence from physics is no evidence they are absent from reality.
- Replying that metal detectors detect part of reality while science detects the whole simply assumes what is in dispute.

Those captivated by science’s success are like the drunk searching only under the streetlamp because that is where the light is.
objections.pushback:
If pressed, “But nothing else has a track record like science,” point out that nothing else is *trying* to do what science does. Logic, mathematics, ethics, and metaphysics don’t aim at technology, just as a spatula doesn’t aim at finding coins.

> One-liner: A metal detector’s perfect record doesn’t prove only metal exists — and physics’ record doesn’t prove only the measurable exists.

objections.title: You trust your cardiologist — so you’re inconsistent to reject scientism
objections.objection: Critics of scientism happily rely on their cardiologist, their mechanic, and their software engineer. Only when science turns to their morals, music, or metaphysics do they cry “scientism.” They want science’s benefits while exempting their own cherished beliefs from its scrutiny.
objections.reply: Feser answers that this is like saying you can’t consistently trust metal detectors to find *anything* unless you believe they alone detect physical objects. Trusting a method within its domain doesn’t commit you to thinking it has no limits. Recognizing that science reliably tells us about hearts and engines is perfectly compatible with holding that there are truths — in logic, mathematics, ethics, and metaphysics — that its methods are not built to capture. To insist otherwise, you must already assume science covers all of reality, which begs the question.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says the difference is that science’s domain *is* everything, ask for the argument for that — and note that it can’t be a scientific one.

> One-liner: Trusting a tool for its job doesn’t mean believing it’s the only tool.

objections.title: What has metaphysics ever predicted? Science covers everything worth knowing
objections.whoRaises: Defenders of scientism in retreat; common in online debate
objections.objection: Grant that science can’t answer every question. The questions it can’t answer produce no consensus and no technology — philosophy just goes in circles. So even if science doesn’t tell us everything, it tells us everything worth knowing. Show me the predictions and inventions of metaphysics or theology.
objections.reply:
Feser gives two replies.

1. **The success is rigged.** If you count as “science” only questions that are predictable, controllable, and capable of consensus, then of course science will be one long success story — like taking only courses you know you’ll ace and then citing your GPA as proof of your brilliance and of the worthlessness of the other courses.
2. **The claim is itself philosophy.** That only scientifically tractable questions are worth pursuing is not a scientific result. Defending it requires exactly the kind of non-scientific reasoning it disparages.

Demanding metaphysics’ predictions is also a category mistake — like demanding the metal-detecting successes of gardening, cooking, and painting, and discarding spades, spatulas, and paintbrushes when none are forthcoming.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic stresses philosophy’s lack of consensus, note that controversy is not the same as failure (Feser’s closing point), and that the very questions “what counts as knowledge?” and “what is worth knowing?” are ones science cannot answer — yet the skeptic is confidently answering them.

> One-liner: Grading science only on the questions it’s built to answer guarantees a perfect score — and “only those questions matter” isn’t a scientific claim.

objections.title: Non-scientific philosophy is mere “conceptual analysis”
objections.whoRaises: James Ladyman and Don Ross (*Every Thing Must Go*) and the program of naturalized metaphysics
objections.objection: If philosophy isn’t simply an extension of natural science, all that’s left for it is conceptual analysis — consulting intuitions and folk notions. But nothing guarantees these track reality. At most they tell us how we happen to think about the world, not how it is. So metaphysical “demonstrations” tell us about our concepts, not about God.
objections.reply:
Feser calls this a false alternative, a variant of **Hume’s Fork** (everything knowable is either a relation of ideas or a matter of fact).

1. **It refutes itself.** The claim that every legitimate inquiry is either natural science or conceptual analysis is neither a conceptual truth nor something science could find evidence for. So the objector occupies a third cognitive stance toward reality in the very act of denying there is one. (Appealing to neuroscience or cognitive science wouldn’t help: that would assume they are our only source of knowledge about cognition, which is the very point in dispute.)
2. **Logic and mathematics break the fork.** Their truths have a necessity empirical science lacks and an objectivity mere concept-mapping can’t guarantee. Denying their necessity or objectivity faces well-known difficulties (chapter 3), and the only motive for it is to rescue scientism.
3. **Natural theology belongs with them.** The truths the proofs establish are, like logical and mathematical truths, necessary and objective, yet neither empirical findings nor mere conceptual relations.

If the scientism advocate can’t see how such knowledge is possible, that’s his problem — he already has oceans of knowledge he can’t account for. He is like a thief caught with the loot who demands the police produce the ownership papers for their squad car.
objections.pushback:
If the objector bites the bullet and denies that logic and math are necessary or objective, ask whether that denial is necessary and objective — and point out that the only reason offered for such a drastic move is to save the theory under examination.

> One-liner: “Everything is either science or mere concept-shuffling” is itself neither — so it falls into the very gap it says doesn’t exist.

objections.title: The laws of physics explain everything — or else nothing ultimately explains anything
objections.whoRaises: Lawrence Krauss (layers of laws); Hawking and Mlodinow; scientism generally
objections.objection: Science explains phenomena by laws of nature, and deeper laws explain shallower ones. That is all the explanation there is or needs to be. If you ask for more — an explanation of the laws themselves — you are asking for something no one can have, so science can’t be faulted for not supplying it.
objections.reply:
Any appeal to laws raises the questions of what a law is, how it has any power to do anything, and where it comes from. Science presupposes laws, so it can’t answer these. Feser surveys the theories of laws and shows none lets them be the ultimate explanation:

- **Aristotelian:** laws describe how things act given their natures — so they presuppose the things and can’t explain why those things (or the universe) exist.
- **Descartes and Newton:** laws are God’s way of ordering things — so God does the real explaining.
- **Humean:** laws just summarize regularities — they say *that* a pattern holds, not *why*; they redescribe rather than explain.
- **Platonic:** laws are abstract objects things participate in — but then we must still explain why there is a physical world participating in them, and in these rather than others.

The fallback “ultimate explanation is impossible anyway” is itself a philosophical claim, not a scientific one — and false, because it violates the principle of sufficient reason (chapter 5).
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says “it’s laws all the way down,” note that an infinite stack of laws, each borrowing its explanatory force from the next, explains no more than a single unexplained law — see the next objection.

> One-liner: Laws describe how things behave; they can’t be what makes there be anything to behave.

objections.title: The fundamental laws are just a brute fact
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Mackie; Bertrand Russell (in his debate with Copleston)
objections.objection: Even granting that science can’t explain its own deepest laws and that philosophy is a genuine source of explanation, there may simply be no explanation of why the fundamental laws are as they are — theological, philosophical, scientific, or otherwise. Everything else is explained by them; they are just there.
objections.reply:
Feser gives three problems.

1. **It contradicts PSR**, which chapter 5 defended. So it is a nonstarter.
2. **It is ad hoc.** Its only motive is to escape arguments like the five proofs — ironic, since atheists accuse theists of tailoring premises to conclusions. An independent motive would exist if Hume’s or quantum mechanics’ challenges to PSR worked, but (as Part A showed) they don’t. And, following Lloyd Gerson: when someone has *offered* an explanation, you can’t reject it by saying “maybe there’s no explanation”; you must show what’s wrong with the one offered.
3. **It drains all laws of explanatory power.** Explaining P by law A, A by law B, and then calling B a brute fact is like resting a book on a shelf, the shelf on brackets, and then letting go of the brackets in midair. A regress of laws is a hierarchical series (chapter 1): it must terminate in something self-explanatory that imparts explanatory power without deriving it. Neither the unexplained nor the explained-by-another can do that — only what is purely actual, without parts, whose essence is existence, and so absolutely necessary.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says the theist also has a stopping point — God — reply that the difference is not whether the regress stops but *where*: God is not a brute fact but self-explanatory, because his essence is existence. A contingent law, which might have been otherwise, can’t play that role.

> One-liner: If the bottom law explains nothing, then nothing resting on it explains anything either.

objections.title: Who designed the designer? A designer is even more complex
objections.whoRaises: David Hume; Richard Dawkins (*The God Delusion*)
objections.objection: Any being able to design a universe would have to be at least as complex as the universe. Complex things need explanations, so the designer would need a cause of its own. Positing it only adds to what needs explaining; a simpler, naturalistic explanation is more probable.
objections.reply:
The objection is aimed at **design arguments** in the style of Paley or Intelligent Design, which infer from complex, precisely arranged structures (eyes, flagella) by analogy with artifacts to a probable designer. The five proofs are nothing like that:

1. **No appeal to complexity.** The Neo-Platonic proof starts from things having parts, but not from how many or how precisely arranged. A pebble or a drop of water — which Paley would never use — works just as well.
2. **No appeal to probability.** The proofs concern hierarchical causes operating here and now, not a linear chain back to the origin of species, and they are strict demonstrations, not inductive or best-explanation arguments. Talk of what is “more probable” or “more parsimonious” misses them; refuting them requires showing a false premise, an invalid step, or a begged question.
3. **Most importantly, they agree with the objection.** A complex cause would need a cause — that is exactly why the proofs conclude that the first cause is absolutely simple, without parts. That is true of the God they reach and of nothing the atheist proposes as the terminus of explanation.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says a mind that knows everything must be complex, note that this assumes God knows the way we do — by many distinct mental items assembled together. Chapter 6 grounds God’s knowledge in his being the cause of all things (like an author conceiving a whole story in one flash) and, through the doctrine of analogy, warns against reading our piecemeal, composite way of knowing into a simple being. This is a course elaboration; Feser’s own reply here doesn’t take up the point. You can also ask which of the skeptic’s own ultimate explanations is simple.

> One-liner: Agreed, a complex cause would need a cause — that’s why the proofs end in something with no parts at all.

objections.title: Go “one god further”
objections.objection: Jews, Christians, and Muslims already reject Zeus, Venus, Thor, Quetzalcoatl, and thousands of other gods. Atheists simply reject one more. To be consistent, monotheists should extend their disbelief to their own God.
objections.reply:
1. **The evidence differs.** There are at least five demonstrations of the God of classical monotheism and no one offers arguments for Zeus. Affirming one while denying the others is no inconsistency — and the critic must answer those arguments rather than lumping God in with the pagan gods.
2. **The deeper problem is a category mistake.** The objection pictures God as one member of a class of supernatural beings, like werewolves and ghosts. But the God of classical theism is in no genus (that would make him composite, while he is simple); shares no essence with other “gods” (that would distinguish his essence from his existence, while he is existence itself); and is not one cause among many but the purely actual source of all causal power — including that of Zeus, were Zeus real. The pagan gods of the stories have bodies, moods, parents, beginnings, ignorance, and vices; each is *a being*. God is not a being that has existence, but subsistent being itself.
3. **Analogies.** An anti-Euclidean who says “you admit drawn triangles have imperfect sides — I just go one step further to triangularity itself,” or an anti-Platonist who says the Form of the Good is imperfect too, has confused a standard with one more instance of what it measures. And this is so *whether or not* Euclid or Plato is right: if they are wrong, it isn’t because triangularity is crooked or the Good is flawed. Likewise, even if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God turned out to be one more nonexistent god.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says, “That’s just redefining God to dodge the objection,” note that this is how classical theists from Aristotle and Plotinus to Augustine, Maimonides, Avicenna, and Aquinas have always understood God — long before anyone raised the objection — and that it is what the five proofs independently conclude to.

> One-liner: Zeus is a character inside the world who may not exist; God is the reason there’s a world at all — rejecting one isn’t a smaller version of rejecting the other.

objections.title: The philosophers’ God isn’t the God people actually worship
objections.whoRaises: Pascal-inspired critics; skeptics and some believers who contrast the “God of the philosophers” with the “God of Abraham”
objections.objection: Even if the arguments prove a purely actual, simple First Cause, that abstraction isn’t the God of ordinary believers — the God they pray to and read about in scripture. So the arguments don’t support the religion people actually practice.
objections.reply:
1. **Irrelevant even if true.** If the arguments succeed, the God of philosophical theism exists and atheism is false. What remains is a debate among theists about whether some religion gives further, revealed knowledge of this God.
2. **Not true.** Some religions explicitly identify the two. Standard Catholic teaching holds that the God of the Bible is the God knowable by philosophical argument: some truths (omnipotence, omniscience) are knowable both by reason and by revelation, others (the Trinity) only by revelation — but it’s one God known two ways. Other religions make similar claims.
3. **The ordinary believer believes in the same God, understood less technically.** He knows nothing of divine simplicity or act and potency, just as the layman knows nothing of quantum fields and pictures molecules as balls and sticks — yet the layman really does believe in atoms. The ordinary believer holds that God is the uncaused, unique, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good cause of the world: the same God, less sophisticatedly grasped.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says “but the God of the Bible gets angry and changes his mind,” note that this is a question of how to interpret scripture — a debate classical theists have long engaged — and that it still leaves atheism refuted if the proofs stand.

> One-liner: If the proofs work, atheism is false either way — and the believer’s God and the philosopher’s God are one God seen with different levels of detail.

objections.title: Evil proves God doesn’t exist (the logical problem)
objections.objection: God is supposed to be omnipotent and perfectly good. An omnipotent being can do anything, and a good being eliminates evil as far as it can. So God would be both able and willing to eliminate all evil. Yet evil exists. So either God isn’t omnipotent, isn’t good, or doesn’t exist. And don’t appeal to free will: God could have made free creatures who always freely choose the good.
objections.reply:
Feser notes that a **defense** (showing evil is compatible with God) suffices here; no full **theodicy** (explaining why God permits each evil) is needed. Using chapter 6’s account of omnipotence and goodness, he targets Mackie’s second premise:

1. **Omnipotence doesn’t include contradictions.** Even God can’t make a round square — not because of a limit on power but because it’s not a *thing* to do. If some goods logically require the permission of certain evils, God can’t have the goods without the evils.
2. **Goodness doesn’t require removing every removable evil.** Removing some evils removes goods that presuppose them. A good parent could end the misery of homework by cancelling it but won’t, since that would sacrifice the child’s learning.
3. **Grant Mackie his free-will point — it still fails.** Feser doesn’t take Plantinga’s route of denying that God could create free creatures who never sin. He grants that such a world, even one with morally significant choices, is possible. But it couldn’t contain all the moral goods of *this* world: forgiveness and mercy require actual wrongdoing; courage requires danger; compassion requires misfortune; sacrifice requires losing something good (cf. Hick’s soul-making). These goods are impossible without evil.

So Mackie’s argument fails — as Mackie himself later conceded. (Feser adds that this is not the claim that ours is the best possible world or that God had to create the best; only that, having made this world, God permits its evils because he draws from them goods not otherwise possible.)
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says, “Surely God could get those goods with *less* evil,” you have moved to the evidential problem (next). You can also note that “less” invites an endless slide — any world with forgiveness and courage will contain some evil that could be imagined slightly smaller.

> One-liner: Some of the best things — forgiveness, courage, compassion — can’t exist in a world with nothing to forgive, fear, or pity; so evil and a good God aren’t contradictory.

objections.title: Pointless suffering makes God improbable (the evidential problem)
objections.objection: Grant that evil doesn’t strictly contradict God. A perfect being would still prevent any suffering it could prevent without losing a greater good or allowing something as bad or worse. Some actual suffering looks exactly like that — a fawn trapped in a lightning-caused forest fire, burned, suffering for days before it dies, with no one to learn courage or compassion from it. We can’t prove no greater good comes of it, but it’s rational to believe none does — and so rational to believe there is no God.
objections.reply:
1. **The inference works only if we lack independent evidence for God.** Believing “there’s probably no greater good here” is rational only if we have no independent reason to think a perfectly good, omnipotent, omniscient God exists — because if we do, we have reason to think there *must* be a greater good even when we can’t see it. The five proofs, plus the arguments for God’s attributes, supply exactly that.
2. **Rowe concedes the key possibility.** He admits a hidden greater good is possible. So he must admit that independent proof of God gives reason to believe such a good is actual.
3. **So it can’t challenge the proofs.** To do so it would first have to refute them independently — and if it could, it wouldn’t be needed.
4. **Our ignorance is to be expected.** If there is an afterlife (Feser defends the soul’s immortality elsewhere), earthly evils could be unredeemable only if no good in an endless life could outweigh them — an absurd claim, since even the worst sufferings here end. And we can no more picture that life than a small child can picture adulthood; children can’t see the point of homework or discipline until they grow up. Given how much greater God is than any parent and how much stranger the afterlife is than adulthood, we should expect both that God can bring an outweighing good and that we can’t yet see how. For a defense, the mere possibility of such an afterlife suffices.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says “that makes theism immune to evidence,” see the objection on unfalsifiability below: the theist’s position can be overturned — by refuting a premise of the proofs. If the skeptic says “an animal has no afterlife, so the fawn’s suffering can’t be outweighed for *it*,” be honest that Feser’s text doesn’t address animal suffering in detail; his core reply doesn’t depend on it: given independent proof of a good God, some greater good is served, whether or not we can identify it.

> One-liner: “I can’t see a reason” becomes “there is no reason” only if you have no independent reason to trust the one who can see — and the proofs give us one.

objections.title: Divine hiddenness
objections.whoRaises: J. L. Schellenberg, *Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason*
objections.objection: A perfectly loving God would want a personal, explicit relationship with each of us, and such a relationship requires believing he exists. So he would make his existence obvious to everyone open to him. But it isn’t obvious — many sincere people don’t believe. So there is no such God.
objections.reply:
The argument rests on two assumptions, and Feser rejects both.

**(1) God would make himself obvious.** Not all theists hold that God seeks a relationship with us — Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover contemplates itself and takes no notice of us — so as a general argument for atheism it’s a nonstarter. Even for Jews and Christians, who rightly (Feser says) believe God does seek relationship, the argument leaves untouched most of what the proofs establish: one, simple, purely actual, immutable, immaterial, eternal, omnipotent, omniscient cause. If that is true, atheism is false. As for God’s goodness and love, the answer parallels the reply to Rowe: given proof of a good, loving God, to whatever extent he hasn’t made himself more obvious, there must be a greater good in it — and there’s no better reason to deny that possibility here than with the fawn.

Hick’s idea of **epistemic distance** — God leaves room for free choice — is exaggerated (the universe isn’t religiously ambiguous; and plenty of believers who never doubted God did terrible things, so free choice doesn’t depend on doubt). But it holds a kernel of truth: God gives us a long leash in what we think as in what we do. Philosophers have denied change, time, matter, causation, free will, the self, even consciousness; unsurprisingly some deny God. Finite minds err, free wills can turn from evidence, and people have motives for doing so.

**(2) God isn’t obvious to most people.** Historically, the vast majority of humans have been theists of some kind, and most still are — often with a confidence atheists complain about. If God is hidden from most people, most people haven’t noticed. That ordinary believers’ reasons are unsophisticated no more makes God hidden than laymen’s crude grasp of science makes scientific truths hidden. Most experts across Western history held God’s existence knowable by argument, and many still do; saying their arguments have been refuted begs the question. If many intellectuals reject God on the basis of incompetent objections like “what caused God?”, their sense that God is hidden says more about their grasp of natural theology than about natural theology.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says, “But *I* have honestly looked and don’t see it,” take that seriously and personally — don’t accuse them of bad faith. Feser’s point is not that every nonbeliever is dishonest, but that finite minds and free choices of attention make error possible for anyone, and that the proofs are available to be examined. Invite them to look at one proof carefully together.

> One-liner: Most humans in history have found God anything but hidden — and where he seems so, finite minds and free attention are enough to explain it.

objections.title: Theistic arguments are just rationalizations
objections.whoRaises: Popular skeptics; frequent in online discussion
objections.objection: Believers decided God exists first and then went looking for arguments. Proofs of God are just after-the-fact rationalizations of conclusions fixed in advance, so they don’t deserve serious attention.
objections.reply:
1. **It’s a fallacy.** This is a textbook ad hominem — **poisoning the well**: rejecting an argument because of the arguer’s supposed motives. Whether an argument is valid and its premises true is completely independent of who offers it or why.
2. **It cuts both ways.** Someone who wants God to exist might avoid scrutinizing atheist arguments; someone who wants God *not* to exist might avoid scrutinizing theist ones. Thomas Nagel candidly admitted that he hopes there is no God and suspected that this “cosmic authority problem” drives much of today’s scientism and reductionism.
3. **So motives settle nothing.** Not all atheists are dishonest, and neither are all theists. The only way to tell whether an argument is good is to examine it — not to look for excuses not to.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says, “But you *do* want God to exist,” you can cheerfully admit it — and ask whether that makes a premise false or a step invalid. Then ask which one.

> One-liner: Why someone gives an argument tells you nothing about whether it’s sound — let’s check the premises instead.

objections.title: It can’t be a “proof” if so many people remain unconvinced
objections.whoRaises: Common skeptical claim; implicit in many philosophers’ treatment of theistic arguments
objections.objection: A real proof would convince any rational person who understood it. But after centuries, many intelligent people who have heard these arguments still reject them. So no one can claim a proof or demonstration of God’s existence.
objections.reply:
Feser gives three replies.

1. **Much of the rejection is uninformed.** Many standard criticisms attack caricatures and show ignorance of what defenders actually said. Rejection by the ill-informed is no evidence of failure.
2. **Double standard.** Skeptics treat any objection to a theistic argument as proof it “fails,” as though a good argument must command universal assent. They never treat arguments for materialism or against free will that way; those stay on the table despite critics. Hume’s objections from two centuries ago are treated as final. (Putnam observed that by this standard the philosophical arguments of Frege, Russell, Quine, Davidson, and Lewis would all fail too.)
3. **It misunderstands “demonstration.”** For classical theists, a demonstration is a deductively valid argument from premises that are certain, their certainty established by metaphysical analysis. That makes it more secure than scientific inference in two ways: it isn’t probabilistic or a best-explanation inference where a rival could be right; and its premises can’t be overturned by future observation, since all observation presupposes them. The Aristotelian proof’s premise that change occurs is empirical in a sense (so not a priori), but any future experience would itself be a change; you might show some apparent change unreal, never that all change is. Its other premises are defended metaphysically — causality via PSR, and PSR by showing that denying it undermines itself.

Nothing about such arguments implies that every reader, even a fair and informed one, will immediately see their force, or that no hard work is needed to defend the premises. Controversy doesn’t mean failure. What a demonstration needs is that, in the end, it can be defended against every objection — and Feser holds the book has done that for all five proofs: Q.E.D.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says “then you’re just claiming victory,” agree that the claim has to be earned premise by premise, and offer to go through any premise they think fails. That is what a demonstration invites.

> One-liner: No major philosophical argument convinces everyone — the question isn’t whether it has critics but whether their objections actually work.

objections.title: “After what happened to me, I can’t believe in God” (the existential problem of evil)
objections.whoRaises: Someone in grief or pain; Ivan Karamazov in Dostoevsky’s *The Brothers Karamazov* is the classic literary voice
objections.objection: This isn’t a syllogism. My child died (or I was abused, or I watched someone waste away). Don’t tell me about greater goods. Any God who would allow this either doesn’t exist or doesn’t deserve worship, and your arguments feel like an insult to what I went through.
objections.reply:
This is a course addition, not a separate objection in Feser’s text, but his treatment equips you for it — if you use it wisely.

1. **First, don’t argue.** Listen. Acknowledge that what happened is genuinely evil — Feser’s own view (chapter 6) is that evil is a real privation, a lack of what ought to be there, not an illusion. Never imply the suffering is secretly fine.
2. **Be honest about the limits of what you know.** Feser offers a *defense*, not a theodicy: he does not claim to know why God permitted any particular evil, and he argues we should *expect* not to know. You can say “I don’t know why this happened” with complete integrity.
3. **When — and only if — they want to talk it through,** the core points are: the reasons for believing God exists don’t depend on understanding this event; if God is real and good, this suffering isn’t the last word; and on the classical view the goods that can come from evil include things like mercy, courage, and compassion, and a future good that no present suffering can match in duration.
4. **Don’t hide behind the argument.** Philosophical compatibility is a real answer to an intellectual objection; it is not a comfort to press on someone mid-grief.
objections.pushback:
If they say, “A God who allowed this isn’t worth worshipping,” you can gently note that this already assumes a real standard of good and evil that the event violates — something the classical theist affirms and the proofs ground — and that the classical God is not a bystander weighing tradeoffs but the source of all goodness, who (on Feser’s view) permits evil only in order to draw a greater good from it. But timing matters more than content.

> One-liner (said gently, and only when welcome): “I don’t know why this happened — but I don’t think it’s the end of the story, and I don’t think you’re wrong to be angry.”

objections.title: Appealing to the proofs makes theism unfalsifiable
objections.whoRaises: Skeptics responding to the reply to Rowe and Schellenberg; critics of “skeptical theism”
objections.objection: Every time evil or hiddenness counts against God, you say, “There must be a greater good we can’t see, because the proofs show God exists.” That makes your belief immune to any possible evidence. A view nothing could count against isn’t rational.
objections.reply:
This is a course extension, applying the logic of Feser’s reply to Rowe.

1. **It’s ordinary reasoning, not special pleading.** When you have strong independent evidence for a claim, apparent counterevidence is reasonably reinterpreted rather than allowed to overturn it. If you’ve proved a theorem, an apparent counterexample tells you to look for your mistake in the counterexample. Rowe himself grants a hidden greater good is possible; the only question is whether we have reason to think it actual.
2. **The view is vulnerable — at the right place.** Feser’s position can be overturned: show that a premise of one of the five proofs is false, or a step invalid. As he puts it in effect, if the evidential argument could refute the proofs independently, it wouldn’t be needed. The objection is welcome to target the proofs directly.
3. **The appeal is limited.** The reply doesn’t claim to explain every evil or to make any claim whatever about God compatible with anything; it applies specifically where the proofs have established God’s goodness, power, and knowledge.
objections.pushback:
If the skeptic says “but you’d never admit a premise was false,” invite them to name one they think is false and test it together. That is exactly how falsification works for demonstrative arguments.

> One-liner: My belief can be refuted — by showing a proof fails; what it can’t be refuted by is our not seeing God’s reasons.

objections.title: “I’m not a scientism fanatic — I just think science is the best method we have”
objections.whoRaises: Moderate naturalists; many scientists and educated laypeople
objections.objection: Nobody really holds the crude view that science is the only source of knowledge. My view is modest: science is our most reliable method, and where it is silent we should suspend judgment. Since science is silent about God, agnosticism or atheism is the reasonable default.
objections.reply:
This modern variant is a course addition, but Feser’s arguments apply straight to it.

1. **“Best method for what?”** Science is the best method for the measurable and predictable. Whether it is the best method for questions about what any measurable world presupposes — change, composition, contingency — is exactly the issue, and it isn’t settled by praising science.
2. **“Suspend judgment where science is silent” is still scientism in disguise.** It is not a scientific result, and applied consistently it would require suspending judgment about logic, mathematics, the reliability of our senses, and the very rule being stated.
3. **Silence is not evidence.** Physics is silent about God for the same reason it is silent about meanings and purposes: its method leaves them out (the airplane engineers).
4. **So engage the arguments.** A moderate who genuinely allows that non-scientific reasoning can yield knowledge has no remaining reason to set the proofs aside unexamined.
objections.pushback:
If they reply, “But philosophy never settles anything,” point to the “worth knowing” objection above — and to the fact that they have just settled a philosophical question (what the default should be) quite confidently.

> One-liner: “Believe only what science shows” isn’t something science shows — so if you allow other kinds of reasoning, let’s actually look at the proofs.

misconceptions.myth: Rejecting scientism means rejecting or downplaying science.
misconceptions.correction: Feser praises the achievements of physics and says its abstractive method is perfectly legitimate. What he rejects is the philosophical thesis that science is the only source of knowledge — a thesis science itself cannot establish. The five proofs start from what science presupposes, not from gaps in it.

misconceptions.myth: Feser claims to know why God permits each particular evil.
misconceptions.correction: He explicitly offers a defense, not a theodicy. He argues only that evil is compatible with God and that, given independent proof of a good God, there must be a greater good even when we can’t identify it — and that our not knowing is exactly what we should expect.

misconceptions.myth: Feser’s reply to evil assumes this is the best of all possible worlds.
misconceptions.correction: He denies that, against Leibniz: God could have created nothing, or a world better in various respects. The claim is only that, having created this world, God permits its evils to draw from them goods that would otherwise be impossible.

misconceptions.myth: The five proofs are sophisticated design arguments, so Dawkins’ complexity objection hits them.
misconceptions.correction: They don’t appeal to complexity, analogy with artifacts, or probability, and they concern hierarchical causes operating now, not biological origins. They conclude to an absolutely simple cause precisely because they agree that complex things need causes.

misconceptions.myth: If physics doesn’t mention colors, purposes, or God, physics has shown they don’t exist.
misconceptions.correction: Physics leaves out whatever can’t be mathematically modeled by methodological design. Its silence is like the airplane engineers’ silence about meal preferences: guaranteed by the method, not a discovery. Physics even implies there is more to reality, since structure must be the structure of something.

misconceptions.myth: The “one god further” objection fails only because there’s better evidence for God than for Zeus.
misconceptions.correction: That’s Feser’s first point, but the deeper one is that the objection is a category mistake: the God of classical theism isn’t a member of any kind, including “gods.” Even if atheism were true, it wouldn’t be because God is one more nonexistent god.

misconceptions.myth: Feser answers divine hiddenness by saying God doesn’t care about us.
misconceptions.correction: He uses Aristotle’s aloof Unmoved Mover only to show the argument isn’t fully general. He himself holds, with Jews and Christians, that God does seek a relationship with us, and answers hiddenness by the greater-good reasoning, by the long leash God gives finite free minds, and by denying that God is actually hidden from most people.

misconceptions.myth: Quoting Nagel’s wish that there be no God shows atheists are intellectually dishonest.
misconceptions.correction: Feser says explicitly that not all atheists (or theists) are dishonest. Nagel’s admission shows only that the motive charge cuts both ways — and therefore settles nothing. Only examining the arguments does.

misconceptions.myth: A real demonstration would convince every rational person who hears it.
misconceptions.correction: No major philosophical argument meets that standard, as Putnam noted. A demonstration is a valid deduction from certain premises; it may take serious work to defend and can be resisted by fair-minded people. What matters is whether it survives every objection.

misconceptions.myth: The ordinary believer worships a different God from the one the philosophers prove.
misconceptions.correction: The ordinary believer holds that God is the unique, uncaused, all-powerful, all-knowing, all-good cause of the world — the same God, understood less technically, just as a layman with a ball-and-stick picture of atoms still believes in atoms.
